column2: reason

No baseline carries a Security channel. `baseline-elevated-win11` vendors one .evtx file, a LanguagePackSetup operational log, whose records agree with none of this rule's three conditions. Fabricating a Security log to give the gate something to measure is what fixtures/hosts/PROVENANCE.md forbids: a baseline is the claim that a machine like this is unremarkable, and an invented one claims nothing.
column3: A baseline carries a Security channel whose records this project is allowed to publish. fixtures/evtx/PROVENANCE.md forbids capturing from a player machine and says why: a Security record routinely carries a user name, a host name, a source IP, a SID and a command line, records cannot be redacted in place because each is checksummed within its chunk, and both the rendered-record and raw-string scans must be run before anything is vendored. So the capture has to come from a Windows 11 installation made for this purpose — throwaway local account, no network sign-in, nothing personal on it — and not from anyone real. MEASURED 2026-09-13 on one real Windows 11 machine (build 26220, elevated scan): its Security channel carried four Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog records with event id 1100, and no 1102. Those agree with this rule on provider and channel and differ on the event id, so a Security log from a machine of that kind confronts this rule at two conditions of three with no clearing having happened. The expectation this row carried before is now a measurement, on one machine. DECIDED 2026-09-14 by the owner: no machine is built for this capture for now. What a baseline would have caught — the rule widened to match what an ordinary Security log holds — is covered instead by the negative fixture `an-ordinary-security-log.json`, whose shape (Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog 1100, and 1101, with no 1102) was measured on two ordinary Windows 11 machines; widening the rule to 1100 was tried and fails `cargo xtask check-rules`. This row stays because that fixture is a specification, not a baseline.

column2: No baseline carries a System channel, for the same reason and with the same one vendored .evtx file as the rule above.
column3: A baseline carries a System channel captured under the same conditions as the rule above, with its PROVENANCE row. MEASURED 2026-09-13 on one real Windows 11 machine (build 26220, elevated scan): across 156 record groups on its System channel, NOT ONE was written by Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog. The doubt this row carried is settled in the unhelpful direction — an ordinary System log does not appear to confront this rule, so vendoring one would not close this row and might show that nothing can. Before capturing anything, check a second machine: if that also holds no Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog record on System, the question to answer is whether this rule can be confronted at all, not which fixture to add. UPDATED 2026-09-14: a second ordinary Windows 11 machine (build 26200, elevated scan) DID hold a Microsoft-Windows-Eventlog record on System — event 30, once — so an ordinary System log can confront this rule at two conditions of three, and the question above of whether it can be confronted at all is answered yes. DECIDED 2026-09-14 by the owner: no machine is built for the capture for now; the negative fixture `an-ordinary-system-log.json` carries that measured shape, and widening the rule to event 30 was tried and fails `cargo xtask check-rules`.

column2: Every baseline with FiveM describes an empty plugins folder, which is what the one real install measured holds (ADR 0035, ADR 0036), so no baseline observation carries a `signature` in `location: plugins`. The one observation that carries both fields, the baseline's FiveM.exe, differs in location and in signature — two conditions, not one. A file written into a baseline plugins folder to give the gate something to measure would be a description of an ordinary machine nobody measured, which fixtures/hosts/PROVENANCE.md forbids.
column3: A baseline's plugins folder holds a file measured on a real machine from a published release — for example what an official ReShade release puts there, hashed and signature-checked from that release's own download — with a PROVENANCE row saying where it came from, the date and the Windows build. Its `signature` answer, whatever it is, confronts this rule or the one beside it. Not a file invented to stand for an ordinary plugin.
